children: Inflation is rising almost 4% a year, PCE shows
Customers shop at a Target in Chicago. Americans are struggling to cope with high inflation, but they're also spending enough to keep the economy growing.

The measure of inflation used by the Federal Reserve to influence U.S. interest rates rose again in October at an accelerated rate, virtually assuring the central bank will increase borrowing costs next month.

The Fed's preferred inflation barometer, known as the PCE index, climbed 0.3% in last month as Wall Street forecast. The increase pushed the yearly rate of inflation up to 3.8% from 3.7% to match a nearly three-year high.
The rate of inflation has been running above the Fed's 2% goal for more than six years, leaving an indelible stain on the U.S. economy and frustrating households and businesses.

The Fed skipped a rate hike in October to get a clearer picture of price trends, but inflation actually got worse. Wall Street almost universally expects the bank to lift a key U.S. interest at its mid-December meeting - and then again early next year.
The Fed considers the PCE, formally known as the personal consumption expenditures price index, as the most accurate gauge of U.S. inflation.
Key details: The Fed pays especially close attention to the core PCE that omits food and energy since it's a better predictor of future inflation. The news in that regard was not any better.
The core rate of inflation also rose 0.3% last month. The yearly rate climbed to 3.3% from 3.1%.

Higher inflation means Americans are paying more for the same amount of goods as services now than they did a few years ago, but consumer spending is also rising faster than inflation in a good sign for the economy.
Consumer spending rose 0.3% last month, merely keeping up with inflation, but forecasters predict a robust increase in the holiday season that officially gets underway after Thanksgiving.
Spending has been buoyed by low unemployment, steady income growth and strong stock markets gains for the wealthy over the past few years.
Incomes aren't keeping up with inflation, however, so spending is sure to suffer unless the Fed manages to drive the rate of inflation below 3%, and soon.

Big picture: The economy has plowed forward despite tariffs, higher oil prices and stubborn inflation, but now comes a new challenge in the form of rising interest rates. Higher borrowing costs tend to slow the economy.
Most economists predict strong U.S. growth in 2027, but that will depend on whether the Fed can corral inflation without needing to jack up interest rates to punishingly high levels.
Market reaction: The Dow Jones Industrial Average DJIA and S&P 500 SPX were set to open lower in Wednesday trades.
